explain.title: What a force does
explain.body: A common concept of a force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the magnitude and direction of velocity of a body. For example, a person pushes or pulls a door to open it.

explain.title: Contact forces
explain.body: A contact force is a force that is exerted by one object on the other at the point of contact. Friction, drag, thrust, normal force, air resistance, tension force and elastic force are examples given in your textbook.

explain.title: Friction and drag
explain.body: It is the force that resists motion when the surface of one object comes in contact with the surface of another. This is the textbook definition of friction. The drag force is the resistant force caused by the motion of a body through a fluid. It acts opposite to the relative motion of any object moving with respect to surrounding fluid.

explain.title: Non-contact forces
explain.body: A non-contact force is defined as the force between two objects which are not in physical contact. The non-contact forces can work from a distance. Gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces are examples.

explain.title: Examples of non-contact forces
explain.body: Gravitational force is an attractive force that exists among all bodies which have mass. An electrostatic force acts between two charged objects. Magnetic force is a force which a magnet exerts on other magnets and magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt.

mistakes: Do not say that every force needs physical contact; gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces can act at a distance.
Do not confuse drag with friction: drag is caused by motion through a fluid and acts opposite to relative motion.
Do not confuse tension with normal force: tension is experienced by a rope when pulled, while normal force is the surface's reaction on an object lying on it.
When listing contact forces, give the number requested and choose forces from the contact-force list.
Use the textbook's stated definitions and examples when answering board questions.

explain.title: Four forces
explain.body:
There are four fundamental forces in nature. These are:

1. Gravitational force
2. Electromagnetic force
3. Strong nuclear force
4. Weak nuclear force

Every force comes under any of these forces. In other words, these four are the basic categories of force.

explain.title: Gravity and electromagnetic force
explain.body:
The gravitational force is the weakest one among all four forces. Being a long range force, it extends to infinite distance although it becomes weaker and weaker.

The electromagnetic force causes the interaction between electrically charged particles. Electrostatic and magnetic forces come under this category. These are long-range forces. Electromagnetic forces are stronger than gravitational and weak nuclear forces. This force causes all chemical reactions and binds together atoms, molecules and crystals.

explain.title: Strong nuclear force
explain.body: It holds the atomic nuclei together by binding the protons and neutrons in the nucleus overcoming repulsive electromagnetic force between positively charged protons. It is also a short-range force with the order of 10⁻¹⁴ m. If the distance between nucleons increases beyond this range, this force ceases to act.

explain.title: Weak nuclear force and unification
explain.body:
Weak nuclear force is responsible for the disintegration of a nucleus. For example, the weak nuclear force executes the β-decay (beta decay) of a neutron, in which a neutron transforms into a proton. In the process, a β-particle (electron) and an uncharged particle called antineutrino are emitted. In other words, we can say that due to weak nuclear force radioactive decay of atoms occurs. It is a short-range force of the order 10⁻¹⁷ m.

The section explains that the weak nuclear force and electromagnetic force can be modelled as two aspects of the same force, called the electroweak force.

mistakes: Do not mix up the roles of the strong and weak nuclear forces: the strong force binds the nucleus, while the weak force is responsible for its disintegration and beta decay.
Do not give the ranges in reverse: the strong nuclear force is of order 10⁻¹⁴ m and the weak nuclear force is of order 10⁻¹⁷ m.
Do not say gravity is the strongest force; the section specifically calls it the weakest of the four.
Do not describe electromagnetic force as acting only in nuclei; it acts between electrically charged particles and is long-range.
Do not omit that the antineutrino emitted in the described beta decay is uncharged.

explain.title: Newton’s first law and inertia
explain.body: Your textbook states: “A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.” This means an object does not change its motion by itself. The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia. Mass measures inertia: a greater mass means greater inertia.

explain.title: Newton’s second law
explain.body: Your textbook states that if a net external force acts on a body, it accelerates in the direction of the force. Acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass. The relation is F = ma. One newton produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a body of mass 1 kg.

explain.title: Force changes velocity
explain.body: A force can produce acceleration or deceleration and so change velocity. Because velocity is a vector, the change may be in its magnitude, direction, or both.

explain.title: Newton’s third law
explain.body: Your textbook states: “For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.” The two forces act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other. For example, when a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.

mistakes: Do not say that action and reaction cancel each other; they act on different bodies.
Use the net or resultant force in F = ma, not just one force when other forces also act.
Do not confuse inertia with force; inertia is a property of a body and depends on its mass.
When using F = ma, write the units: force in newtons, mass in kilograms, and acceleration in m s⁻².
Do not claim that a force can only change speed; it can change direction too.

explain.title: Mass
explain.body: The simplest definition of mass is that it is a measure of the quantity of matter in a body. Scientifically, mass is a scalar quantity and remains the same everywhere. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg), and an ordinary balance measures mass.

explain.title: Scientific definition of mass
explain.body: The characteristic of a body which determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a certain force acts upon it is known as mass of the body.

explain.title: Weight
explain.body: Weight is a gravitational force acting on the object. It is a vector quantity directed downward, towards the centre of the Earth. The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts the body towards its centre.

explain.title: Gravitational field and weight
explain.body: The gravitational field is a space around a mass in which another mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction. The gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on unit mass. Weight is given by w = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength. Its value is 10 N kg⁻¹. Since g varies from place to place and with altitude, weight can change; mass stays the same. Weight is measured in newtons (N) using a spring balance.

mistakes: Do not say that an object's weight is measured in kilograms; kilograms are the unit of mass and newtons are the unit of weight.
Do not treat mass and weight as the same quantity: mass is scalar and stays the same, while weight is a vector force that depends on g.
Do not use Earth's value of g when a question gives a different value, such as the Moon's gravitational acceleration.
Do not omit the unit N from a calculated weight.

explain.title: Mechanical balances
explain.body: A mechanical balance consists of a rigid horizontal beam that oscillates on a central knife edge as a fulcrum. It has two end knife edges equidistant from the centre. Two pans are hung from bearings on the end knife edges. Put the object in one pan and standard weights in the other, then adjust the weights until the beam is in equilibrium.

explain.title: Platform balances
explain.body: A mechanical platform balance is used for heavy items such as flour bags, cement bags, and steel bars. Its fulcrum is very near one end of the beam, so smaller weights can balance the load. These smaller weights have already been calibrated to standard weights.

explain.title: Electronic balances
explain.body: An electronic balance does not need standard weights. It must be connected to a power supply, although some models use dry-cell batteries. It displays the mass, and some models can display the total price if the rate per kg is entered.

explain.title: Force meters
explain.body: A force meter is a scientific instrument that measures force. It is also called as a newton meter or a spring balance. It measures force directly in newtons (N), unlike balances, which measure mass in kilograms or its multiples.

explain.title: How an ordinary force meter works
explain.body: An ordinary force meter has a spring, a handle, a hook, a pointer, and a scale in newtons. The pointer coincides with zero when nothing is hung from the hook. Hanging an object makes the spring compress or stretch, and the pointer indicates the object's weight.

mistakes: Do not say that a balance measures force in newtons; balances measure mass.

explain.title: Friction opposes motion and dissipates energy

explain.body: The friction between two solid surfaces is called sliding friction which can be divided into two categories. Static friction acts when a pull tends to move an object but it remains at rest. When the object slides, the friction is known as kinetic friction.

explain.body: As a falling object gets faster, air resistance increases. explain.title: Rolling friction and reducing friction

explain.title: What is a system?
explain.body: The collection of objects is known as a ‘system’. If no external force acts on any object of the system, it is known as isolated system.

explain.title: Conservation of momentum

explain.title: Momentum can transfer

explain.title: Recoil

explain.title: Impulse and safety

explain.title: Force and motion
explain.body: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion or shape. The resultant force is the combined effect of all forces on the object.

explain.title: Newton's laws

explain.title: Momentum and impulse
explain.body: Momentum is p = mv. Impulse is force multiplied by the time for which it acts, and equals the change in momentum. Increasing the time of a collision reduces the force for the same momentum change.

explain.title: Conservation of momentum

explain.title: Friction

notes.answer: A force is a push or pull that can start, stop or change an object's motion.
notes.explanation: A force is a push or pull. It can change how an object moves, and forces are either contact or non-contact forces.
notes.simple: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion. Some forces need objects to touch; others act from a distance.

notes.answer: The four fundamental forces are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
notes.explanation: The four fundamental forces are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear. They explain the basic interactions in nature.
notes.simple: Nature has four basic kinds of force. Each force has a different job and range.

Link strong nuclear force with holding the nucleus together.

notes.checkAnswer: Strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together.

notes.title: Drawing a Free-Body Diagram
notes.answer: A free-body diagram is used to show the relative magnitudes and directions of all the forces acting on an object in a given situation.
notes.explanation: A free-body diagram shows the forces acting on one object. It uses arrows to show the direction and relative magnitude of each force, and labels to name each force.
notes.simple: Draw the object as a box. Add an arrow for every force acting on it, point each arrow in the force's direction, and label it.
examples: A book pushed to the right across a table has an applied force to the right and friction to the left.
The table exerts a normal force upward on the book, while the book's weight acts downward.
steps: Represent the object by a box.
Draw each force arrow outward from the centre of the box.
Point each arrow in the direction of the force.
Use arrow length to show the force's relative magnitude.
Label each arrow with the exact type of force.

notes.checkAnswer: The book has an applied force to the right, friction to the left, a normal force upward, and weight downward.

notes.title: Newton’s Laws of Motion
notes.answer: Newton’s first law describes inertia; the second law is F = ma; the third law says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
notes.explanation: Newton’s laws explain how forces affect motion. The first law describes how an object resists a change in its motion, the second law links force to mass and acceleration, and the third law says forces between two interacting bodies are equal and opposite.
notes.simple: A force can change motion. Objects resist changes to their motion, and when two objects interact, each pushes or pulls the other.
examples: When a bus stops suddenly, passengers tend to move forward because their bodies tend to keep moving.
When a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.
steps: Use the first law to describe what happens when no net external force acts.
Use F = ma when a question gives mass and acceleration, or asks for force.
For the third law, identify the two interacting bodies and state the equal, opposite forces acting on them.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do action and reaction forces not balance each other?
notes.checkAnswer: The forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other.

notes.title: Limitations of Newton’s Laws
notes.answer: Relativistic mechanics is applicable to elementary particles having velocities close to the speed of light.
notes.explanation: Newton’s laws describe everyday motion very accurately, but they are not exact for every situation. For very small particles or objects moving close to the speed of light, relativistic mechanics is needed.
notes.simple: Newton’s laws work very well for ordinary things we see and use. For tiny particles or extremely fast objects, Einstein’s relativistic mechanics is more suitable.
examples: A car moving at an ordinary road speed is well described by Newton’s laws.
An elementary particle moving close to the speed of light needs relativistic mechanics.
steps: Use Newton’s laws for objects and speeds we meet in everyday life.
Recognise that they are not exact for all types of motion.
For elementary particles moving close to the speed of light, use relativistic mechanics.
notes.checkAnswer: Newton’s laws are a good approximation for everyday motion, but are not exact for very small objects or objects moving close to the speed of light.

notes.title: Mass and Weight
notes.answer: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object: w = mg.
notes.explanation: Mass tells us how much matter an object contains and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on the object, so it can change when gravitational field strength changes.
notes.simple: Mass is how much matter is in something. Weight is the pull of gravity on it.
examples: A person with a mass of 80 kg has a weight of 800 N on Earth when g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
The same person has a weight of 128 N on the Moon when g = 1.6 m s⁻².
steps: Write the relation: w = mg.
Put in the mass and the value of g.
Multiply to find the weight, and give the answer in newtons.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the weight of a 2 kg object where g = 10 N kg⁻¹?
notes.checkAnswer: Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same; weight is a gravitational force measured in newtons and can change with g.

notes.title: Balances and force meters
notes.answer: A force meter, also called a newton meter or spring balance, measures force directly in newtons (N).
notes.explanation: Mechanical and electronic balances measure mass. A force meter measures force directly in newtons. An electronic balance needs a power supply or, in some models, dry-cell batteries; it does not need standard weights.
notes.simple: Balances measure mass; a force meter measures force.

A force meter can show the weight of an object in newtons.

notes.checkQuestion: Which instrument measures force directly in newtons?
notes.checkAnswer: A force meter measures force directly in newtons (N).

notes.title: Friction and its effects
notes.answer: Friction opposes motion. Static friction acts before surfaces start sliding; kinetic friction acts while they slide; rolling friction acts while an object rolls. Air resistance can balance gravity and produce terminal velocity.
notes.explanation: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces. It can slow moving objects and change some of their energy into heat. The main types in this section are static friction, kinetic friction and rolling friction.
notes.simple: Friction is a force that resists motion. It can slow things down, warm surfaces, and make it harder for objects to slide.
examples: A cricket ball slows down on the ground because friction acts opposite to its motion.
A wheel rolls more easily than an object slides because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
steps: Identify the surfaces or fluid involved.
Decide whether the object is at rest, sliding, rolling or falling through air.
Name the friction or resistance acting on it.
State how that force affects the object's motion.

notes.title: Momentum and Impulse
notes.answer: Impulse is the total change in momentum of an object when a large force acts on it for a short time.
notes.explanation: Impulse measures the change in an object's momentum when a force acts on it. A force acting for a longer time can produce the same change in momentum with a smaller average force.
notes.simple: Impulse tells us how much an object's momentum changes during a force. More time for the change means less average force.
examples: A cricketer draws his hands back while catching a ball to increase the time of impact and reduce the force on his hands.
Packing materials increase the time over which a fragile object slows down, reducing the force on it.
steps: Find the object's mass and velocity.
Calculate momentum using p = mv.
For a force acting over time, use F = Δp/Δt.
For an impact, calculate the change in momentum as final momentum minus initial momentum.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the average force if the same change in momentum takes place over a longer time?
notes.checkAnswer: Impulse is the total change in momentum of an object when a large force acts on it for a short time.

notes.title: Conservation of Momentum
notes.answer: If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.
notes.explanation: In an isolated system, the total momentum before an interaction stays equal to the total momentum after it. Use signs to show direction: if an object moves in the opposite direction, its velocity is negative.
notes.simple: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. When no external force acts on a system, its total momentum does not change.
examples: A gun and bullet start at rest, so their total momentum is zero. After firing, the bullet's forward momentum is balanced by the gun's backward momentum.
When two balls stick together after a collision, add their masses to find the moving mass after collision.
steps: Write the law: total momentum before = total momentum after.
Choose a positive direction and give opposite velocities negative signs.
Substitute each object's mass and velocity before and after the interaction.
Solve for the unknown and include its direction in the answer.
notes.checkQuestion: What stays equal before and after a collision in an isolated system?
notes.checkAnswer: The total momentum before and after the collision is equal.

notes.title: Dynamics: forces, motion and momentum
notes.answer: Dynamics studies forces and their effects on motion.
notes.explanation: A force can change an object's motion. Newton's laws explain how forces affect motion, while momentum and impulse help us study collisions and recoil. Friction opposes motion between surfaces.
notes.simple: A force is a push or pull that can change motion. Momentum depends on mass and velocity.
examples: A 10 kg block pushed by a 5 N force has acceleration 0.5 m s⁻².
When a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.
steps: Find the resultant force acting on the object.
Use F = ma to find acceleration, or use momentum change where appropriate.
For collisions in an isolated system, equate total momentum before and after.
Include units and direction in the final answer.

notes.checkAnswer: The block accelerates at 0.5 m s⁻².
